Đakovo Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Đakovo, Croatia

Not demolished. Đakovo, first mentioned in 1239 as a bishop's residence and later under 150 years of Ottoman rule (called 'Yakova'), rebuilt as a craft and farming center after Turkish defeat in 1687; by 1910 it had 6,304 residents. Jews from Slovakia and Moravia settled there through the 19th century, organizing formally in 1852 and building a synagogue in 1880; the Hevra Kadisha followed in 1861. Population reached 407 by 1921. Relations with other residents were notably warm - the local bishop, Anton Akshmoviz, held honorary Hevra Kadisha membership. During WWII, roughly 200 local Jews were caught up in a much larger tragedy: a nearby concentration camp held about 3,000 women and children (mostly Jewish) from across Croatia in brutal conditions until July 1942, when survivors were transferred to Jasenovac and murdered; men were sent directly to Jasenovac. By war's end, no Jews remained in Đakovo, and the synagogue became a concert hall. This cemetery, established in 1860 (or 1879, per differing sources), includes a neo-Romanesque Ceremonial Hall from 1879 and holds tombstones from 1881 to 1998; women and children who died in the nearby camp were buried separately in the municipal cemetery in 1942, individually marked, with a postwar Holocaust memorial added.
